# Cūḷajanakajātaka (Ja 52)

**ID:** Ja 52
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷajanakajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Shorter Tale of King Janaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja52

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷajanakajātaka* (Ja 52) is a short narrative of the Pali Jātaka collection, rendered in English as *The Shorter Tale of King Janaka* [SuttaCentral]. According to the nidāna preserved in the commentary, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at Jetavana with reference to a backsliding monk who had abandoned active striving (*ossatthaviriya*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Rather than detailing the Bodhisatta's background, the commentary defers the entire extended narrative to the later, extensive *Mahājanakajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877; Fausböll 1897].

The single verse (*gāthā*) of the jātaka is spoken by King Janaka as he sits beneath the royal white parasol (*setacchatta*), extolling relentless perseverance: a wise person should continue to strive and never despair, drawing from the Bodhisatta's own experience of surviving a shipwreck and seeing himself brought out of the water onto dry land (*vāyameth' eva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito / passāmi vo 'ham attānaṁ udakā thalaṁ ubbhatan ti*) [Fausböll 1877]. At the conclusion of the teaching, the discouraged monk attained arahantship, and the Buddha identified the past King Janaka as himself [Fausböll 1877].

No internal Pali text reuse or cross-language parallels are reported for this text in either SuttaCentral or DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Beyond the textual tradition, the *Cūḷajanakajātaka* is attested in Southeast Asian epigraphic and artistic records; for instance, it is depicted on an eleventh-century terracotta plaque at the Ananda Temple in Pagan with the Mon inscription *culajanaka jāt 52* [Schober 1997].
